name: Classical Chinese
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Of course, if monosyllables can carry stresses independently, then this means that monosyllables must have a bimoraic structure; otherwise, there would be no stresses. [...] It is well known that most function words in Old Chinese have yin-type rhymes, which either occupy the unstressed positions or are prosodically invisible constituents. They are usually monomoraic. (p. 131) [...] the tone system, to a certain degree, rejects monosyllabic feet; it also means that the existence of monosyllabic feet can be guaranteed in the Old Chinese where there was no tone. (p. 138)
new_statements.citation: Zhuang, Huibin, Pusong Zhao & Shengli Feng. 2025. Foot-shift and disyllabification in the history of Chinese: with a revisit of syllabic structures of Old Chinese. Language and Linguistics 26(1): 123-154. doi:10.1075/lali.00173.zhu.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source gives a word-stress placement rule for Literary Chinese. For the underlying Old Chinese: (a) it is reconstructed as toneless (Sagart 1999: 'Old Chinese was a toneless language'; Sagart & Baxter 2017 sec. 2.3); (b) words were monosyllables or sesquisyllables whose loosely attached presyllables are 'iambic' (Sagart & Baxter 2017 sec. 2.4; Sagart & Baxter 2012) and, per Ferlus 2012: 7, 'inaccentuées' (unstressed), i.e. prominence on the main/final syllable; (c) the Feng school (Zhuang, Zhao & Feng 2025) treats each heavy OC monosyllable as a bimoraic foot able to bear stress, with light CV function words unstressed, and dates tones and disyllabic feet to Han and later. Middle Chinese and all modern reading traditions are tonal (Handel 2003: MC four lexical tones; Eno 2012: Literary Chinese now read in Mandarin).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Zhuang et al.: function words (mostly yin-type/CV rhymes, e.g. 吾 vs stressed 我) are unstressed or 'prosodically invisible'; a light syllable in a stressed position can be lengthened. Ferlus: presyllables do not follow main-syllable sound laws because unstressed.
new_statements.domain_note: All statements concern reconstructed Old Chinese phonological words (monosyllable or presyllable+main syllable), argued from rhyme, meter and reconstruction, not from speech; Zhuang et al. also discuss phrase-level nuclear stress in Classical Chinese syntax. Literary Chinese citation forms are read in the compiler modern (tonal) language.
new_statements.identity_note: lite1248 is Literary/Classical Chinese, a written register with no native phonology of its own: it is read today in the compiler vernacular (Eno 2012: iii, 'is now read in Mandarin'), and every phonological statement located concerns either reconstructed Old Chinese (Glottolog oldc1244; the Shijing-to-Han spoken language underlying the classical corpus) or the Middle Chinese Qieyun reading tradition (midd1344; four lexical tones per Handel 2003 glossary). The stress-related statements quoted (Zhuang, Zhao & Feng 2025; Ferlus 2012; Sagart & Baxter 2017 'iambic' presyllables) are all about reconstructed Old Chinese, not about Literary Chinese as such. The Zhuang et al. file is held by the project, not duplicated into lite1248/.

sources.citation: Zhuang, Huibin, Pusong Zhao & Shengli Feng. 2025. Foot-shift and disyllabification in the history of Chinese: with a revisit of syllabic structures of Old Chinese. Language and Linguistics 26(1): 123-154. doi:10.1075/lali.00173.zhu.
sources.quote: Of course, if monosyllables can carry stresses independently, then this means that monosyllables must have a bimoraic structure; otherwise, there would be no stresses. [...] It is well known that most function words in Old Chinese have yin-type rhymes, which either occupy the unstressed positions or are prosodically invisible constituents. They are usually monomoraic. (p. 131) [...] the tone system, to a certain degree, rejects monosyllabic feet; it also means that the existence of monosyllabic feet can be guaranteed in the Old Chinese where there was no tone. (p. 138)
sources.note: pp. 131-134, 138-140: Old Chinese analysed as a (bi)moraic-foot language; heavy monosyllables can bear stress on their own, most function words (CV, yin-type rhymes) 'occupy the unstressed positions or are prosodically invisible'; 吾 light vs 我 heavy/stressed; OC 'where there was no tone'; after Han, tones plus disyllabic feet replace moraic feet. No placement rule within polysyllables.

sources.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 2012. Remarques sur la pharyngalisation en chinois archaïque (Old Chinese) dans le système Baxter-Sagart. 25e Journées de Linguistique de l'Asie Orientale, Paris. HAL halshs-00978164.
sources.note: p. 7: 'les présyllabes étant inaccentuées, leur évolution n'obéit pas aux lois phonétiques de la syllabe principale' - OC presyllables of sesquisyllabic words are unstressed (main/final syllable prominent); passing remark, not a description.

sources.citation: Sagart, Laurent & William H. Baxter. 2017. Old Chinese Phonology: a sketch. Encyclopedia of Chinese Language and Linguistics vol. 3, 274-280. Leiden: Brill. Authors' HAL deposit hal-03892358.
sources.note: Sec. 2.3: 'The dominant view today is that Old Chinese had no tones' (tones from *-ʔ and *-s); sec. 2.4: presyllabic onsets with a central vowel correspond to Sagart 1999's 'loosely attached or "iambic"' preinitials; notes the type A/B distinction was once analysed 'as reflecting different stress conditions (Pulleyblank 1973)'. No word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Sagart, Laurent. 2017. Word Families. Encyclopedia of Chinese Language and Linguistics. Brill. HAL hal-03946651.
Eno, Robert. 2012. Introduction to Literary Chinese, Part One. Open course primer (Indiana University); archive.org item wenyan-primer-v-1.
sources.note: Pronunciation guide p. iii: 'Although originally read in the pronunciation of the vernaculars of its times, Literary Chinese is now read in Mandarin'; appendix: 'growing consensus that Old Chinese was probably not a tone language'. Silent on word stress.

sources.citation: Sagart, Laurent & William H. Baxter. 2012. Reconstructing the *s- prefix in Old Chinese. Language and Linguistics 13(1): 29-59. HAL hal-00781153.
sources.note: Mentions the 'iambic (minor syllable with schwa) variant' of prefixes, referring to Sagart 1999 on iambic prefixes; no stress rule.

sources.citation: Handel, Zev J. 2003. Appendix A: A Concise Introduction to Old Chinese Phonology. In James A. Matisoff, Handbook of Proto-Tibeto-Burman, 543-576. UC Publications in Linguistics 135. Berkeley: University of California Press (eScholarship qt19d79619).
sources.note: Overview of OC syllable structure, initials, finals and tone ('We have no direct evidence that there were phonemic tonal contrasts in Old Chinese'; glossary: 'Middle Chinese had four distinct lexical tones'). Silent on stress/accent.

sources.citation: Duanmu, San. 1999. Stress and the development of disyllabic words in Chinese. Diachronica 16(1): 1-35. doi:10.1075/dia.16.1.03dua (author's preprint from websites.umich.edu/~duanmu/).
sources.note: Metrical account of word length assuming left-headed (trochaic) word/compound stress for Chinese generally; notes flexible mono~disyllabic word length already in classical Chinese (Guo 1938) and disputes that classical spoken Chinese was mostly monosyllabic; no statement of stress placement for Old/Classical Chinese.

sources.citation: Sagart, Laurent. 1999. The origin of Chinese tones. Proceedings of the Symposium Cross-Linguistic Studies of Tonal Phenomena: Tonogenesis, Typology and Related Topics, Tokyo, 91-104. HAL halshs-00096904.
sources.note: Conclusion: 'Old Chinese was a toneless language. Tones arose between Old Chinese and Early Middle Chinese (that is between 500 BCE and 500 CE) as a result of the loss of final laryngeals.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Karlgren, Bernhard. 1926. Philology and Ancient China. Oslo: Aschehoug (Instituttet for Sammenlignende Kulturforskning, Serie A VIII). archive.org DLI scan;ernet.dli.2015.282588.
sources.note: Calls the tones 'the musical accent' of Chinese words (in a passage on romanizing modern Pekinese); nothing on Classical Chinese word stress.
